'''''Calathea''''' is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Marantaceae]]. They are commonly called '''calatheas''' or (like their relatives) '''prayer plants'''. About 200 species formerly assigned to ''Calathea'' are now in the genus ''[[Goeppertia]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Molecular Phylogeny and Redefined Generic Limits of ''Calathea'' (Marantaceae) |year=2012 |last1=Borchsenius |first1=Finn |last2=Suárez |first2=Luz Stella Suárez |last3=Prince |first3=Linda M. |journal=Systematic Botany |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=620–635 |doi=10.1600/036364412X648571 |s2cid=84276716 }}</ref> Calathea currently contains around 60 species. [[native plant|Native]] to the [[tropics|tropical]] Americas, many of the species are popular as [[houseplant|pot plants]] due to their decorative leaves and, in some species, colorful [[inflorescence]]s. The young leaves and [[bract]]s can retain pools of water called [[phytotelma]]ta, that provide habitat for many invertebrates.<ref>Jalinsky, J., T.A. Radocy, R. Wertenberger, & C.S. Chaboo. 2014. Insect diversity in phytotelmata habitats of two host plants, Heliconia stricta Huber (Heliconiaceae) and Calathea lutea Schult (Marantaceae) in the south-east Amazon of Peru. Journal of the Kansas Entomological Society 87(3): 299–311.</ref>

== Description ==
=== Foliage ===
Calathea leaves are often large and colorfully patterned.<ref name="Striking">{{Cite web|title=How to Grow Striking Tropical Calathea|url=https://www.thespruce.com/grow-calathea-indoors-1902745|access-date=2019-04-25|website=The Spruce|language=en}}</ref> The leaves are often variegated with bright colors such as pink, orange, red, and white.<ref name=":0">{{Citation|last=Van Huylenbroeck|first=Johan|chapter=Calathea|date=2018|chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-90698-0_13|title=Ornamental Crops|pages=301–318|editor-last=Van Huylenbroeck|editor-first=Johan|series=Handbook of Plant Breeding|place=Cham|publisher=Springer International Publishing|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-90698-0_13|isbn=978-3-319-90698-0|access-date=2021-11-16|last2=Calsyn|first2=Evelien|last3=Van den Broeck|first3=Andy|last4=Denis|first4=René|last5=Dhooghe|first5=Emmy|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref> The underside of their leaves are frequently purple.<ref name=":0" /> During the night, the leaves fold up.<ref name="Striking" /> In the morning, the leaves unfurl in search of the morning sun.<ref name="Striking" /> This phenomenon, known as [[nyctinasty]],<ref name="Striking" /> is made possible by a small joint the plant possesses between the stem and leaf, called a [[pulvinus]].<ref name=":0" />

=== Flowers ===
Calathea flowers can be yellow, purple, and white and bloom in the summer.<ref name="Striking" /> The flowers have an [[Asymmetry|asymmetrical]] structure with three [[petal]]s and three free [[sepal]]s.<ref name=":0" /> Calathea bracts are often more attractive than its flowers.<ref name=":0" />

== Cultivation ==
In suitable conditions, calatheas can grow up to three feet in height with wide leaves. Though they are slow growers, once they reach their ultimate height they will stop growing.

=== Light ===
Like the shady floors of the tropical canopies, this genus prefers low to medium light.<ref name="Striking" /> Too much direct sunlight can damage their fragile leaves. Too much sun exposure may result in sunburn or dullness in the color of the leaves.<ref name="Striking" />

=== Temperature and humidity ===
Along with low to indirect light preferences, these plants require high [[humidity]] to mimic their natural habitat.<ref name="Striking" /> Some calatheas are placed in  bathrooms, kitchens, and other areas with high-moisture levels.<ref name="Striking" /> Calatheas prefer temperatures 60 °F / 15 °C and above to support healthy growth.<ref name="Striking" /> These plants are also sensitive to cold air. The ideal temperatures range for these plants is 75 °F / 23 °C to 85 °F / 29 °C.<ref name="Striking" />

=== Water ===
Calatheas should be kept moist but not wet.<ref name="Striking" /> Over or under watering these plants can lead to brown, dry leaves.<ref name="Striking" /> Calathea are sensitive to minerals found in tap water such as [[chlorine]] and [[fluoride]].<ref name="Striking" />

=== Growing medium ===
Ideal soil conditions for calatheas should be porous and well draining.<ref name="Striking" /> Drainage is very important for calatheas due to [[root rot]]. A light porous soil and pot with a drainage hole will ensure the plant's delicate root system is not over-watered. Calatheas prefer the soil to be moist but not overwatered. The species also prefers an acidic soil pH.

=== Houseplants ===
The species was first introduced as a houseplant in the 1970s and 1980s.<ref name=":0" /> Over the years, calatheas have become a popular houseplant because of their attractive leaves.<ref name="Striking" /> Calathea are also grown outdoors in Hawaii and southern Florida.<ref name="Striking" /> Unlike their wild counterparts, few indoor-kept calathea will flower.<ref name="Collecting">{{Cite web|date=2018-11-09|title=Calathea: A Guide to Collecting Calathea|url=https://leafandpaw.com/2018/11/08/calathea-a-guide-to-collecting-calathea/|access-date=2019-04-25|website=Leaf and Paw|language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Propagation ===
[[Plant propagation]] is the process of creating an offspring of a plant through a mother plant. Calathea achieve propagation through division.<ref name="Collecting"/> To successfully propagate a calathea, one needs to have a healthy established mother plant. After removing the mother plant from its pot, the plant can be gently separated into smaller parts.<ref name="Collecting"/> Once the calathea has been successfully divided, each new grouping must be planted in its own (well-draining) pot. The newly established calathea will soon shoot out new leaves and continue to grow.

== Native uses ==
In its native range, the large and tough leaves are popular for holding small items. Sometimes, they are used unprocessed, e.g. to wrap [[fish]] for transport in parts of [[Brazil]], such as the [[Benevides, Brazil|Benevides]] region of [[Pará]] {{citation needed|date=November 2021}}. In other places, the leaves are used in [[handicraft]] to produce containers, such as the [[quiver]]s of the [[Nukak]] people of [[Colombia]] {{citation needed|date=November 2021}}. Most famous, perhaps, are the decorative ''Calathea''-leaf [[rice]] containers produced in some villages of [[Thailand]], especially in Ban Huak ([[Amphoe Si Bun Rueang]]) where they are an important source of income and sold to locals and tourists alike {{citation needed|date=November 2021}}.

''Calathea'' foliage is of importance to some [[herbivore]]s, such as the [[caterpillar]]s of the [[purple owl]] (''Caligo beltrao'') which feed on ''[[Calathea zebrina|C. zebrina]]'' {{citation needed|date=November 2021}}. For a list of ''Calathea'' diseases, see [[List of foliage plant diseases (Maranthaceae)|List of foliage plant diseases (Marantaceae)]].

Due to [[habitat destruction]], several species are threatened with [[extinct]]ion {{citation needed|date=November 2021}}.

== Native regions ==
